title: Knights of Doom!
summary: Sacrifice the rook to draw a knight into the mating net, then use a king waiting move against a second underpromotion.

nodes.question: Should White defend the rook or offer it with check?
nodes.explanation: Black’s king has reached c1. The pawn on b2 threatens promotion, while Na1 can fork a rook on c2.

nodes.question: Does another knight promotion stop the win?
nodes.explanation: The rook has been sacrificed. The white knights on b3 and d5 cover the king’s escapes, and Kf1 prepares a mating net around Kd1.

branches.title: Sacrifice, close the net, then wait
commentary: Begin after ...Kc1 in the seven-piece phase. The earlier eight-piece setup and first underpromotion remain source context.
Rc2+ offers the rook with check. White forces Black to address the king attack instead of simply promoting.
Nxc2 accepts with the knight from a1, drawing it into the final mating arrangement.
Nb3+ checks from d4 and covers a1, c1 and d2. The other white knight stays on d5.
Kd1 is the illustrated escape. Returning to b1 would allow Nc3 mate.
Kf1 closes e1 and e2. White threatens Nc3 mate against the confined king.
b1=N underpromotes again. The new knight controls c3, so the immediate mating jump can be captured.
Kf2 is the waiting move. It covers e1 and e2 from a different square, putting Black to move while its knights must preserve the defense.
Nca3 moves the c2 knight to the square shown in the saved frame. The automatic captions say c3 here, but that is not a legal knight move from c2. The b1 knight stays in place to guard c3.
Ne3# switches the mating square. The black king on d1 is checked by Ne3; Nb3 covers c1 and d2, Kf2 covers e1 and e2, and neither black knight can remove the check.
branches.explanation: Ne3# switches the mating square. The black king on d1 is checked by Ne3; Nb3 covers c1 and d2, Kf2 covers e1 and e2, and neither black knight can remove the check.

branches.title: The black king returns to b1
commentary: Compare the source’s king retreat toward b1 after the rook sacrifice.
Rc2+ sacrifices the rook with tempo.
Nxc2 removes the rook but places the black knight where it does not prevent White’s mating jump.
Nb3+ forces the king to choose its next square.
Kb1 steps back into the corner arrangement covered by the two white knights.
Nc3# gives actual mate. Nc3 checks b1 and covers a2 and c2; Nb3 covers a1 and c1. Black’s b2 pawn blocks another flight square.
branches.explanation: Nc3# gives actual mate. Nc3 checks b1 and covers a2 and c2; Nb3 covers a1 and c1. Black’s b2 pawn blocks another flight square.

branches.title: Promote to a queen instead
commentary: Compare a queen promotion after White has played Kf1.
b1=Q gains maximum material but does not guard c3 or give check against Kf1.
Nc3# is actual mate against Kd1. The knight on b3 covers c1 and d2; Kf1 covers e1 and e2. The new queen cannot capture the checking knight or interpose against a knight check.

exercises.prompt: Why give the rook away instead of preserving it?
exercises.answer: Rc2+ draws Na1 to c2 with tempo, allowing Nb3+ and Kf1 to form the mating net before Black can use a queen.
The new knight guards c3, so White changes the move order. Kf2 keeps the king’s escape squares covered and leaves Black to move; the illustrated ...Na3 then permits Ne3 mate.
